name: Budapest Puppet Theatre
intro: The Budapest Bábszínház is the capital's professional puppet theatre, based on Andrássy út in Terézváros. It grew out of the State Puppet Theatre founded in 1949 and took its present name in 1992. Its resident company plays for small children and also for teenagers and adults, on a main stage, a studio and a further small room.
about: The Budapest Bábszínház, or Budapest Puppet Theatre, stands at Andrássy út 69 in the sixth district. According to its own website it is a non-profit company run by the Budapest city government together with the national ministry responsible for culture. The director since 2020 is Ellinger Edina, and the company also has a literary head, a drama pedagogue and a resident ensemble of actors.

The repertoire is deliberately wide. The theatre’s site lists children’s productions such as Babaróka and Boribon és Annipanni, among others, next to titles for older audiences, among them Frankenstein, Peer Gynt and a new staging of Az ember tragédiája. The company describes its approach as puppet-based thinking: actors learn puppetry techniques alongside live acting, and the puppet structures are redeveloped again and again. The programme changes with each season, so any list of titles is only a snapshot.

The official venues page names three playing spaces. The main stage and the Ország Lili Stúdió, which is on the fourth floor, are both in the main building at Andrássy út 69. A third room, the Kemény Henrik Terem, is outside the main building at Vörösmarty utca 31.

Alongside performances the theatre runs a participatory programme called Mozgató, with theatre-pedagogy sessions and workshop groups, as well as a summer camp and an overnight event for children aged ten to twelve called Éjszaka a Bábszínházban. For visitors, the theatre is a lively cultural stop on one of the city’s grandest avenues. Which language a performance is given in, and which age group it suits, should be checked on the official page for each title.
tips: Check the theatre’s official website for the current programme, the recommended age of each show, the language of each performance and which of the three venues it is played in.
Note the two addresses: the main stage and the studio are at Andrássy út 69, while the Kemény Henrik Terem is at Vörösmarty utca 31. Check the official contact page for how to get there.
Andrássy út is lined with other sights, from the opera house to the House of Terror, so a performance can easily be combined with a walk along the avenue.
Ask the theatre about its rules on photography and recording before you plan to film a performance, and read the house rules on arrival; the workshops and camps have their own information pages.

history.intro: The company’s story begins in the first years after the Second World War, when professional puppetry in Budapest was organised as a state theatre, and it has since moved between two buildings and changed its name once.

sections.heading: The State Puppet Theatre of 1949
paragraphs: The theatre’s own history page dates the start of the professional puppet theatre to October 1949 and names Bod László as its first director. Hungarian Wikipedia says the Állami Bábszínház, the State Puppet Theatre, was formed in September 1949 from the Mesebarlang ensemble, so the sources differ by a month on the exact start.

The company played at Andrássy út 69, a site that had earlier held the Régi Műcsarnok, the old art gallery, and then the Nemzeti Kamaraszínház. Its audience at first was children only; plays for adults were added from 1951.

sections.heading: Designers, directors and a protected corner of the arts
paragraphs: A We Love Budapest article notes that the theatre sheltered artists who did not fit the socialist realism expected by communist cultural policy, and says this freedom from censorship lasted mainly for about four years after 1949. Ország Lili worked as set and costume designer from 1960 until her death and later led the painting workshop; Bródy Vera is named as the creator of the Mazsola and Misi Mókus puppets.
Szilágyi Dezső directed the theatre from 1958 to 1992, a span of 34 years according to the official history page.

sections.heading: Jókai tér, a new building and a new name
paragraphs: The company used the house at Jókai tér 10 from 1971 and came back to a new building on the old Andrássy út site in December 1976. Hungarian Wikipedia says the Jókai tér room then carried on as the institution’s chamber theatre.
In 1992 the State Puppet Theatre became the Budapest Bábszínház. Meczner János took over as director in 1994 and held the post until 2020, when Ellinger Edina succeeded him.

name: Napraforgó Street Experimental Housing Estate
address: Napraforgó utca, Pasarét, Budapest II district
intro: Napraforgó utca in Pasarét, on the Buda side of the II district, is a short street of modernist family houses laid out as an experiment in 1931. Most of the houses were designed by different architects, so the flat roofs, large windows and garden terraces vary from plot to plot. The houses are private homes, best admired from the pavement.
about: Napraforgó utca, Sunflower Street, is known in Hungarian as the Napraforgó utcai kísérleti lakótelep, the experimental housing estate, and its original name was the Pasaréti úti kislakásos mintatelep, a model estate of small dwellings. Hungarian Wikipedia says the street carries house numbers 1 to 22 and was named in 1931.

What makes it interesting is the variety. Most of the houses were designed by different architects, so the forms differ considerably. Nearly all the houses have a ground floor and one upper floor, with No. 3 as the exception, since it has two upper floors. Typical features are flat roofs, large windows and terraces opening onto the gardens from the ground floor or the upper floor. Kozma Lajos’s twin house at Nos. 6 to 8 is partly clad in clinker brick. The style is described as modern, in the spirit of the Hungarian adaptation of the Bauhaus.

The heritage register lists No. 9, a twin house designed by Kertész K. Róbert and built in 1931, as a monument (entry 300), with other houses of the estate listed close by. A We Love Budapest article adds that some owners have restored their homes following monument-protection requirements.
Everything here is a private home. There is no museum and no entry, so the estate is a place for a quiet stroll along the street in residential Pasarét.
tips: Treat it as a street walk: the houses are lived in, so stay on the public pavement, keep noise down and do not photograph residents or look over fences into gardens.
Houses are best read as a group. Look for the contrasts between neighbours, for example the clinker brick of Nos. 6 to 8 and the three-level No. 3 among the otherwise two-level houses.

The memorial stone in the middle of the street lists architects by house number, but Hungarian Wikipedia says it gets the numbers and pairings wrong in several places, so treat the attributions with caution.

No official visitor information is published for the estate; if you want a guided architectural walk or to see an interior, check the programmes of local heritage and architecture organisations instead of knocking on doors.

history.intro: The estate was a private initiative with entrepreneurial capital, not a state project, built to test a question that housing reformers were asking across Europe at the time.

sections.heading: A model estate on the Stuttgart pattern
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the idea came out of the international architecture congress held in Budapest in 1930. At a housing discussion of the Magyar Mérnök- és Építész-Egylet someone suggested building a group of well-matched villas after the Stuttgart Werkbund estate. Ifj. Masirevich György, Kaffka Péter, Kozma Lajos and Vágó László took the idea up, and the building firm Fejér és Dános became the builder.

The Lechner Knowledge Centre mentions the estate in passing in its biography of Virgil Borbíró (Bierbauer), who designed No. 4. It says a city-planning conference in 1931 concluded that modern family houses should be built within planned estates, and that several people then pressed for a model estate to be built.

The experiment asked whether a detached family house with a garden could be designed on a plot of only 100 square fathoms. In July 1930 the Fővárosi Közmunkák Tanácsa allowed plots of that size, on condition that no more than a quarter of each plot be built on.

sections.heading: Inauguration in November 1931
paragraphs: The site of roughly one hectare was divided into plots for family and twin houses. Hungarian Wikipedia counts 16 family houses and three twin houses, 22 dwellings in all, while other popular accounts speak simply of 22 houses. The estate was inaugurated on 9 November 1931 as the Pasaréti úti kislakásos mintatelep.

Hungarian Wikipedia quotes contemporary press reports, among them an admiring one. The builders complained that the authorities had strung overhead power lines on tarred poles instead of burying the cable, and one hostile article mocked that request.

sections.heading: The architects
paragraphs: More than twenty architects, aged 23 to 64, worked on the estate, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. It says only Molnár Farkas had studied at the Bauhaus in Weimar, while the younger architects Masirevich, Fischer József and Molnár belonged to CIAM, the international modernist congress. Among the corrected attributions are Vágó László at Nos. 1 and 11, Kozma Lajos at Nos. 5 and 6 to 8, Kertész K. Róbert at No. 9 and Hajós Alfréd at No. 17.
One later change is recorded: a footbridge that linked the street with Pasaréti út was demolished at the residents’ request.

name: Tétény Plateau Nature Reserve
address: Tétényi-fennsík, Budapest XXII district (southern edge of the Buda Hills, next to Törökbálint)
intro: The Tétényi-fennsík is a protected plateau on the south-western edge of Budapest, in the XXII district, where dry rocky grassland shelters rare plants and insects. It is a nationally protected nature reserve in the care of the Duna-Ipoly National Park, and the Anna-hegy lookout tower just over the border in Törökbálint gives views across it.
about: The Tétényi-fennsík Természetvédelmi Terület is a nature reserve on the southern edge of the Buda Hills. The Duna-Ipoly National Park Directorate’s page says it was declared a protected natural area of national importance by decree 129/2011 (XII. 21.) VM, with a total protected area of 147.78 hectares, lying in Törökbálint and Budapest’s XXII district. Together with the 111 hectares protected locally in 1999, Hungarian Wikipedia counts nearly 300 protected hectares on the plateau.

The reason for the protection is its dry, rocky grassland. The park page names feather grasses (Stipa pulcherrima and Stipa eriocaulis) as the dominant grassland species in places, together with rarer plants such as Colchicum arenarium, which the page calls unique in the Buda Hills, Daphne cneorum, Iris arenaria and Pulsatilla grandis. The plateau is also rich in arthropods, including a Mediterranean-type spider community with several species rare in Hungary and the highly protected insects Colias chrysothome and Isophya costata. Hungarian Wikipedia counts about 400 plant species, 45 of them protected or strictly protected.

The landscape is open and gently stepped. Hungarian Wikipedia gives an average height of about 200 metres, with Anna-hegy (267 m, in Törökbálint) the highest point and Vadász-hegy at 227 m the highest point inside Budapest. It describes Mediterranean gravel and sand layers covered by thick limestone.

For visitors the plateau is a quiet walking landscape rather than a sight with facilities. Wikipedia reports a nature trail created in 2005 and a tourist path to Anna-hegy, where the lookout tower stands in Törökbálint, outside Budapest. A hiking article on We Love Budapest describes it as a large steel-framed tower with views over Törökbálint, the Buda Hills, the Tétényi plateau and Budaörs, and on a clear day across the Danube to Pest. The park’s page does not publish visiting rules or trail information, so access conditions should be confirmed with the directorate.
tips: The Duna-Ipoly National Park page gives no access, trail or visiting information, so contact the directorate or check its website before you go.
Stay on the paths, do not pick plants and take your rubbish with you: the park page names restricting traffic and preventing illegal waste dumping among its aims.

The Anna-hegy lookout tower is in Törökbálint, not in Budapest, and is a steel structure; the We Love Budapest walk from Törökbálint is one way to reach it, but its author advises downloading the route first.
The plateau is open grassland, so dress for the weather, bring water and check the park directorate for any seasonal restrictions.

history.intro: The plateau’s grassland is partly a product of people: centuries of grazing kept it open, and the twentieth century added military use, dumping and building pressure before protection took hold.

sections.heading: Pasture, military use and dumping
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia infers a mosaic of oak woodland, shrub and rock grassland as the original cover. Once the woods were cleared, centuries of grazing kept the plateau open and helped the steppe species survive. The twentieth century added decades of military use and, in the 1990s, illegal dumping.

sections.heading: Protection in 1999 and 2011
paragraphs: In summer 1999 the Budapest municipal assembly designated 111 hectares as a local nature conservation area, known as the Érd-Tétényi plató and also a Natura 2000 site; the XXII district section was cleared and protected in that year. In December 2011 a further 148 hectares were placed under national protection by decree 129/2011.

Wikipedia also records that in spring 2001 the vegetation of the former Mechanikai Művek site was largely destroyed during housing development, that construction later stopped after a change of ownership, and that nature is now regenerating.

sections.heading: Conservation today
paragraphs: The park page lists the aims of the protection as preserving slope-steppe habitats, protecting rare species, restoring native vegetation and reducing non-native trees and shrubs. Wikipedia names invasive species such as tree of heaven, black pine and white acacia as targets and says that the Zöld Jövő Környezetvédelmi Egyesület and the Magyar Madártani és Természetvédelmi Egyesület run habitat management programmes on the plateau.

name: Budapest Cog-wheel Railway (tram 60)
address: Városmajor terminus (Szilágyi Erzsébet fasor) to Széchenyi-hegy, Gyermekvasút, Budapest XII
intro: The Budapest cog-wheel railway, now officially tram line 60, climbs from Városmajor in District XII into the Buda Hills as far as Széchenyi-hegy. The first train ran in 1874, and the line is operated by BKV within the public transport network. Its upper terminus lies beside the Children's Railway, which makes the ride a scenic way into the hills.
about: The Budapesti fogaskerekű vasút runs between Városmajor and the stop named Széchenyi-hegy, Gyermekvasút. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its length as about 3.7 km, with a height difference of 315 m between the terminus at the top and the one at the bottom after the 1890 extension, a maximum gradient of 110 per mille and about ten stops. Journey times between the two ends run from around 14 to 23 minutes, depending on direction. It is a rack railway, so the trams cling to the slope with a toothed rail between the running rails.

BKV’s page for its special vehicles says the line runs to a timetable all year round, that passengers need a valid line ticket and that bicycles can be carried with a validated ticket or a pass that includes the bicycle sticker. The lower terminus is two stops from Széll Kálmán tér on tram 59, and the upper terminus is a short walk from Normafa, where several hiking trails meet; use a route planner to check current connections.

The line has formally been tram route 60 since 21 August 2008. Seven SGP twin units serve it. Hungarian Wikipedia says they have run on a timetable since 1973, whereas a BKK development page calls them about 40 years old and costly to maintain. A preserved Ganz locomotive and trailer, converted for 1,500 V by 2025, are kept for nostalgia runs, according to Hungarian Wikipedia.

The line has had interruptions in recent years, and service patterns, including trips run only on request at the edges of the day, have changed. Check BKK for the current situation before building a plan around it.
tips: Before you travel, check the BKK website or the FUTÁR app for the current timetable and any suspension or replacement bus service; the line was out of service for a long winter break in 2022 to 2023, and BKK has published plans to rebuild and extend it.
BKV says a valid line ticket is needed and that bicycles are carried only under its stated conditions, so check the official ticket and bicycle rules before you board.
At the top, the stop is next to the Children’s Railway station, and BKV points out a short walk to Normafa, where hiking trails meet, so the ride combines naturally with a walk in the Buda Hills.
The lower terminus at Városmajor is reached from Széll Kálmán tér on tram 59, according to BKV; check a route planner for current connections.
Bring a layer: the hills are cooler than the city, and the ride is a hillside transport route rather than a sightseeing tour with commentary.

history.intro: Budapest’s cog-wheel railway is nearly 150 years old and has been rebuilt more than once, changing from steam to electric traction and from one rack system to another.

sections.heading: Riggenbach’s rack line of 1874
paragraphs: The line goes back to Niklaus Riggenbach, designer of the Vitznau–Rigi railway, who applied for it in 1873 in the name of a Basel company, the Internationale Gesellschaft für Bergbahnen, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The first train ran on 24 June 1874. It was a single steam-worked track of about 2.9 km on the Riggenbach rack system, running from Ecce homo rét, today’s Városmajor, up to Svábhegy.

sections.heading: Extension and electrification
paragraphs: On 17 May 1890 the line was extended to Széchenyi-hegy, which brought it to about 3.7 km. After the city took over the operating company in 1926, modernisation began in 1927, and the line reopened as an electric railway on 2 July 1929 with Rowan-system trains. A full rebuild in 1972 introduced the Strub rack and raised platforms; the Ganz trains then ran until 15 March 1973, and SGP articulated units replaced them from 20 August 1973.

sections.heading: Closures and plans for the future
paragraphs: Wikipedia reports that the line was suspended from 11 November 2022 to 1 April 2023, citing high operating costs relative to ridership. BKK’s notice of the reopening describes the winter break as a period of track work, including replacing several hundred metres of track and fitting new switches at the Orgonás stop.

BKK’s development page describes plans to rebuild the track and extend it in both directions, to Széll Kálmán tér and to a new terminus in the central area being developed at Normafa. It says the design plans are finished and that BKK is seeking funding, but it gives no construction start date, so the extension should be regarded as a plan rather than something visitors can ride.

name: Székesfehérvár Ruin Garden (Coronation Basilica memorial)
intro: The Medieval Ruin Garden in Székesfehérvár, in Fejér county, is a national memorial site on the ruins of the royal basilica where Hungarian kings were crowned and buried. King Stephen began the church around 1018. The site is run by the Szent István Király Múzeum, whose pages give current visiting arrangements.
about: The Középkori Romkert, or Medieval Ruin Garden, stands at Koronázó tér in Székesfehérvár and is run by the Szent István Király Múzeum. It preserves the remains of the Virgin Mary basilica, the church that King Stephen founded and that served for centuries as the coronation and burial place of Hungarian kings. It has the status of a national memorial site (Nemzeti Emlékhely).

The heritage register describes the site as a ruin garden, a stone collection and the Szent István mausoleum. Visitors find the foundation walls and plinths of the basilica and medieval carved stonework within a rectangular enclosure bounded by streets, buildings and walls. Along the north and east sides run a brick wall with niches and arcaded parts, partly attached to the former inner castle wall, together with a stylised mausoleum and a three-arched gateway. The sanctuary is left open to the sky, and a translucent roof covers the south part of the nave. The register also lists the St Stephen sarcophagus.

A tourism listing for the site adds that an ossuary holds bones excavated from the basilica, about a thousand individuals in all, and that wall paintings by Aba-Novák Vilmos and reliefs by Madarassy Walter decorate the memorial. The museum’s exhibition page mentions Aba-Novák’s historical painting among its permanent displays.

Székesfehérvár lies outside Budapest, in Fejér county, so a visit is a day trip rather than a city stop. Confirm the current visiting arrangements with the Szent István Király Múzeum before planning a journey.
tips: Check visiting arrangements before you go: a tourism listing and museum.hu have given differing information on whether the garden is open to visitors, so confirm with the Szent István Király Múzeum before travelling.
Plan the day around transport from Budapest and check current train and bus information before you go.

The ruins are easiest to understand with some background on the basilica: read about King Stephen, the coronations and the later destruction before arriving, because much of the site consists of foundation lines and fragments.

Béla III and his wife, whose tomb was found in 1848, were reburied in Budapest’s Matthias Church in 1862, so the Matthias Church in the Castle District is a natural pairing for anyone interested in the story.

history.intro: The basilica was one of the central places of the medieval Hungarian kingdom, and the garden that now marks it is a twentieth-century creation on a site that had been largely destroyed centuries earlier.

sections.heading: Stephen’s basilica and the coronations
paragraphs: Until the Ottoman capture in 1543 the town was where Hungarian kings were crowned and many were buried, and the regalia and the royal archives were kept there, according to the MNB and Hungarian Wikipedia. Hungarian Wikipedia gives the construction period of the basilica as 1018 to 1543, and the tourism listing says work on the three-aisled church began around 1018. Stephen was buried there when he died in 1038, and Stephen and his son Imre were canonised in 1083. Wikipedia lists coronations from 1038 to 1527, with Béla IV as an exception, and sources give about fourteen or fifteen rulers buried there.
A tradition recorded by the MNB dates the town’s foundation to 972 under Géza, Grand Prince of the Hungarians; this is tradition rather than documented history.

sections.heading: Ottoman occupation and destruction
paragraphs: The Ottomans captured Székesfehérvár in 1543 and looted the royal tombs. When Christian forces retook the town in 1601, the south-west tower, which the Ottomans were using as a gunpowder store, was blown up. The ruins were afterwards used as a quarry, and by about 1800 the last remains above ground had been demolished. In 1848 workers digging a canal found the tomb of King Béla III and his wife; the remains were reburied in the Matthias Church in Budapest in 1862.

sections.heading: From ruin garden to national memorial site
paragraphs: The garden took shape between 1936 and 1938, according to the MNB. The tourism listing says it opened in 1938, designed by Lux Géza, with wall paintings by Aba-Novák Vilmos and reliefs by Madarassy Walter; the museum notes that this was the year marking the 900th anniversary of King Stephen’s death. A law of 2011 made it a national memorial site.
